summary: Describes how the Domain Name System can store data tied to E.164 telephone numbers and resolve those numbers into URIs that can be used in call setup. It also covers identifying services associated with a number. It is a proposed standard and obsoletes RFC 3761.

plainLanguage.summary: ENUM gives telephone numbers a web-style address. A number such as +44 20 7946 0148 is turned into a domain name under e164.arpa, and the DNS records stored there say which services that number can be used for, such as a SIP address for internet calling. This document defines that lookup and the rules for filling in and reading the records.

subtitle: Giving telephone numbers a domain name, so the DNS can say which services they reach.

tldr.problem: Telephone numbers in the E.164 format have no built-in way to find the internet services, such as a SIP address for internet calling, that belong to the same subscriber.
tldr.mechanism: ENUM turns an E.164 number into a domain name under e164.arpa by reversing its digits, then looks up NAPTR records in the DNS. Records that carry the E2U service field yield URIs, and non-terminal records can point on to another domain.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 3761 and mostly adds clarifications, collected from deployment experience, to fix interoperability problems between clients and provisioning systems.

today: RFC 6116 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2011. It obsoletes RFC 3761 and has not been obsoleted or updated since, so it remains the standard for mapping E.164 telephone numbers to URIs through the DNS.

sections.title: What ENUM Does
sections.content:
This document discusses the use of the Domain Name System for storing data associated with E.164 numbers, the international format defined in ITU Recommendation E.164, and for resolving those numbers into URIs that can be used, for example, in telephony call setup. It also describes how the DNS can be used to identify the services associated with an E.164 number, and includes a Dynamic Delegation Discovery System (DDDS) application specification as detailed in the RFC 3401 series. It obsoletes RFC 3761.

Using the process defined here, E.164 numbers can be transformed into DNS names. Using existing DNS services, such as delegation through NS records and queries for NAPTR resource records, one can look up the services associated with that number. This takes advantage of standard DNS architectural features of decentralized control and management of the different levels in the lookup process.

The domain e164.arpa has been assigned to provide an infrastructure in the DNS for storage of data associated with E.164 numbers. To facilitate distributed operations the domain is divided into subdomains. Holders of E.164 numbers who want them listed in the DNS should contact the appropriate zone administrator as listed in the policy attached to the zone, and one should start looking for this information by examining the SOA resource record associated with the zone, just as in normal DNS operations. As with other domains, policies for such listings are controlled on a subdomain basis and may differ in different parts of the world.

The same mechanisms could be used for other kinds of digit strings, such as numbers in private dialing plans. If they are, the domain apex used for the translation MUST NOT be e164.arpa, to avoid conflict with this specification. The Application Unique String used with dialing plans SHOULD be the full number as specified, without the leading '+' character, which is used to distinguish E.164 numbers in international format from dialed digit strings. For example, to address the E.164 number +44-3069-990038 a user might dial "03069990038", "00443069990038" or "011443069990038"; these strings differ from one another, but none of them start with the '+' character. Implementers and operators of systems using these techniques for other purposes MUST NOT describe them as "ENUM", because the initial "E" stands for E.164.
sections.plainLanguage: ENUM lets a phone number be looked up in the DNS, the same system that turns names into addresses. A number is turned into a domain name, and the records under that name say which services belong to it. The document also explains why the same trick cannot be used for other digit strings without changing the domain.

sections.title: The Application Unique String
sections.content:
The Application Unique String is a fully qualified E.164 number minus any non-digit characters, except for the '+' character that appears at the beginning of the number. The '+' is kept to provide a well-understood anchor for the string, so that it can be told apart from other telephone numbers that are not part of the E.164 namespace.

For example, the E.164 number could start out as "+44-116-496-0348". To ensure that no syntactic sugar is allowed into the Application Unique String, all non-digits except for the '+' are removed, yielding "+441164960348".
sections.plainLanguage: Before the lookup, the number is tidied into a standard form. Every character that is not a digit is removed, except the plus sign at the front. The plus sign stays because it marks the number as an international one, so it cannot be confused with a number dialed inside a country.

sections.title: Turning a Number into a Domain Name
sections.content:
The First Well Known Rule converts the Application Unique String into an initial key, which is used as an index into the application's rules database. For ENUM that database is the DNS, so the key is a fully qualified domain name. The string is converted into a domain name by a four-step algorithm: remove all characters except the digits, so "+442079460148" becomes "442079460148"; reverse the order of the digits, giving "841064970244"; put a dot between each digit, giving "8.4.1.0.6.4.9.7.0.2.4.4"; and append the string ".e164.arpa." to the end and interpret the result as a domain name.

The E.164 namespace and the database are organized so that it is possible to go directly from the name to the smallest granularity of the namespace, so no further processing is needed to generate the initial key.

This domain name is used to request NAPTR records. Each record may contain the end result, or, if its flags field is empty, it produces a new key in the form of a domain name that is used to request further NAPTR records from the DNS. The output of the last loop of the algorithm is a Uniform Resource Identifier in its absolute form.
sections.plainLanguage: The cleaned number is turned into a domain name in four steps: strip the plus sign, reverse the digits, put a dot between each digit and add the e164.arpa suffix. The result is read like any other domain name, and the DNS records under it hold the services.

sections.title: The NAPTR Records and the E2U Service
sections.content:
Only one database is specified for this application: the DNS, which uses the NAPTR resource record to hold the rewrite rules, with keys encoded as domain names. The character set used for the substitution expression is UTF-8, the allowed input characters are all those allowed anywhere in an E.164 number, and the characters allowed in a key are those currently defined for DNS domain names.

The database contains a flags field that signals when the algorithm has finished. At present only one flag, "U", is defined, meaning that the rule is the last one and the output of the rule is a URI. A client that meets a record with an unknown flag MUST ignore it and move to the next rule, and that test takes precedence over any ordering, since flags control the interpretation placed on the fields. If the flag is not present the rule is non-terminal, and the result produced by a non-terminal rule MUST be a fully qualified domain name that the client uses as the new key in the next round of the algorithm.

The service parameters appear in the Services field of the NAPTR record that holds a terminal rule; where the record holds a non-terminal rule the Services field SHOULD be empty and clients SHOULD ignore its content. The syntax is a fixed "E2U" prefix, used to denote ENUM-only rewrite rules in order to mitigate record collisions, followed by one or more Enumservices, each introduced by a '+' character. Each Enumservice has a type of up to 32 characters drawn from letters, digits and '-', optionally followed by subtypes introduced by a colon, each with the same length limit.

More than one Enumservice may be associated with a single NAPTR. Such a compound NAPTR shares the same Regexp field and so generates the same URI, and could be used to indicate a mobile phone that supports both "voice:tel" and "sms:tel". A compound NAPTR can be treated as a set of NAPTRs that each hold a single Enumservice; the reconstructed NAPTRs share the same ORDER and PREFERENCE values but should be treated as if each had a logically different priority, with a left-to-right priority assumed.

Enumservices are registered through the process in RFC 6117, which is not open to any Enumservice that has '-' as the second character of its type string, so the "X-" facet is reserved for experimental or trial use and cannot be registered by the normal process. Any Enumservice type that starts with the facet "P-" is intended for private networks only, will never be registered, and must not be provisioned in any system that answers DNS queries from entities outside that private network. A client that is not sure it is connected to the private network concerned MUST discard such a NAPTR.
sections.plainLanguage: Each record says whether it is the last one in the chain and which service it offers. The service names come after a fixed E2U marker, and a record may list several of them. Two markers are reserved: X- for experiments that cannot be registered, and P- for private networks that must never be published on the public Internet.

sections.title: An ENUM Service Example
sections.content:
The example zone holds three NAPTR records for the domain 3.8.0.0.6.9.2.3.6.1.4.4.e164.arpa. The first says the domain is preferably contacted by SIP, the second by H.323 for voice, and the third by SMTP for messaging. The Enumservice tokens "sip", "h323" and "email" are Enumservice types registered with IANA, and they have no implicit connection with the protocols or URI schemes of the same names. In all cases, the next step in the resolution process is to use the resolution mechanism for each protocol, specified by the URI schemes sip, h323 and mailto, to know what node to contact.

In the first two records the expression matches only queries made for the telephone number +441632960083, while in the last record it matches any Application Unique String value. The first record also shows how the matched pattern can be used in the generated URI. Note that where NAPTR resource records are shown in DNS master file syntax, each backslash must itself be escaped using a second backslash; the DNS packet on the wire has only a single backslash in each case.
sections.plainLanguage: The worked example holds three records for one number: reach it by SIP first, by H.323 second, and by email third. The first two match only that number, while the third matches any number, which is how a catch-all mail contact is written.

sections.title: Lessons from Deployment
sections.content:
ENUM is a DDDS application, and DDDS is designed to be flexible, which opens the possibility of differences of interpretation. This section covers the ENUM-specific interpretation of the DDDS specifications, with the goal of ensuring interoperability between ENUM clients and the provisioning systems that populate domains with E2U NAPTRs. The recommendations reflect an analysis of how implementations behave and the interoperability issues that have arisen.

Case sensitivity was not mentioned at all in RFC 3761, but has been seen as an issue during interoperability test events since then, and there are many case-sensitive clients in current deployment. The only place where NAPTR field content is case sensitive is in any static text in the replacement part of the Regexp field, where case must be preserved when generating the record output; elsewhere case sensitivity is not used. Clients that use the Internet to send their queries, the so-called Public ENUM scenarios, MUST use case-insensitive processing. Clients that operate within closed networks, the so-called Infrastructure ENUM scenarios, can be designed with case-sensitive processing, because all the zones provisioned within such closed networks usually have a known capitalization for ENUM record string content.

For provisioning systems: ENUM NAPTRs SHOULD NOT include characters outside the printable US-ASCII range unless it is clear that all the clients they are designed to support will process them correctly, and non-printable characters SHOULD NOT be used because clients may need to show the content to a person. The case-sensitivity flag is inappropriate for ENUM and SHOULD NOT be provisioned. Registrants and their provisioning systems SHOULD NOT rely on clients taking only the lowest ORDER and PREFERENCE values into account, and SHOULD place in the zone only contacts they are willing to support, since even a record with the worst values may be selected by a user. All E2U NAPTRs SHOULD hold a default value in the ORDER field, and a value of 100 is recommended. Multiple NAPTRs with identical ORDER and identical PREFERENCE values SHOULD NOT be provisioned unless they are truly identical. The '!' character SHOULD be used as the Regexp delimiter, and a literal '+' in the expression field MUST be escaped. Non-terminal NAPTRs SHOULD NOT be provisioned unless it is clear that all the clients in the environment can process them, and a provisioning system SHOULD NOT configure more than 5 such NAPTRs to be processed in one query. Zones MUST NOT be provisioned with NAPTRs in the obsolete syntax of RFC 2916.

For clients: discarding a NAPTR SHOULD NOT end the whole query, and processing SHOULD continue with the next record. Clients MUST sort the records of a retrieved set using the ORDER and PREFERENCE fields, with ORDER as the major sort term and PREFERENCE as the minor one, both with the lowest value first. A client SHOULD NOT discard a record until it has been considered, or until a record before it in the evaluation sequence has been accepted. Records with identical ORDER and PREFERENCE values SHOULD all be accepted and processed in the order they appear in the response. The ORDER value SHOULD only be used when sorting within a single set, not across the sequence of queries created by following non-terminal references. A client that meets a compound NAPTR and cannot process one of its Enumservices SHOULD ignore that Enumservice and continue with the next, discarding the record only if it can handle none of them, and those conditions SHOULD NOT be treated as errors. Clients MUST be ready to process records with a different delimiter character, with non-trivial expression patterns and with many back-reference patterns, and SHOULD discard a record that has more or less than 3 unescaped delimiter characters in the Regexp field.
sections.plainLanguage: The document collects what real deployments learned about how clients and zone operators disagree. It tells zone operators which characters and orderings to use, and tells clients how to sort the records, when to drop one, and when to keep looking rather than give up.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
ENUM uses the DNS, which in its current form is an insecure protocol, so there is no mechanism for ensuring that the data one gets back is authentic. As ENUM is deployed on the global Internet it is expected to be a popular target for attacks, and attacking the DNS infrastructure is one way of attacking the ENUM service itself. A deployed ENUM service SHOULD include mechanisms to mitigate these threats, and most of them can be solved by verifying the authenticity of the data with DNS Security (DNSSEC). Others, such as denial-of-service attacks, cannot be solved by data authentication; the threats include not only the NAPTR lookups themselves but also the records needed for the services to be useful, for example NS, MX, SRV and A records.

Even with DNSSEC deployed, a service should not blindly trust that an address it retrieved is valid and that the entity it connects to is the peer it intended to reach. A service SHOULD always authenticate the entity it connects to during the service setup phase, and not rely on address or identity data retrieved outside that service. Software implementing ENUM must be prepared to receive DNSSEC and other standardized DNS security responses, including large responses and other EDNS0 signalling, and unknown resource records.

The DNS architecture makes extensive use of caching at intermediary nodes. The propagation time for a change in a record approaches the time to live of that record, and there may be several records involved in resolving a target, with changes that are not synchronized, so a change in one of them may cause inappropriate decisions. Given that DNS Update can introduce quite rapid changes in different zones, these transient states may become important. Systems provisioning this data SHOULD take care to minimize changes and to consider the respective time to live values and lease times, and users of the data should detect and recover from unintended session attempts.

Where several providers offer call routing and number or name translation services, any system that lets users change routing or supplier information may give incentives for unauthorized changes. Such environments should be designed with adequate mechanisms for identifying and authenticating those requesting changes and for authorizing them. Finally, many security issues have to do with the resolution process itself and the use of the URIs it produces; those have to be specified in the registration of the Enumservice used.
sections.plainLanguage: The DNS does not prove that the records it returns are genuine, so an ENUM service should use DNSSEC where it can. Even then, a service should check who it is talking to when it connects, rather than trusting the address it looked up.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 3761
sections.content:
This document is an update of RFC 3761, which was edited by Patrik Faltstrom and Michael Mealling. A section has been added explaining the way in which DDDS is used with this specification, and the recommendations in it were collected from experience of ENUM deployment. Differences of interpretation of the DDDS specifications led to interoperability issues, and the clarifications are intended to ameliorate interoperability.

The clarifications include a default value for the ORDER field and for the Regexp delimiter character, required use of the Replacement field in non-terminal NAPTRs, and that string matching is case insensitive. The other substantive changes are the removal of the discussion of registration mechanisms, which is now specified in RFC 6117, the correction of an existing error by adding '-' as a valid character in the type and subtype fields of the service parameters, and the addition of the "P-" private service type.
sections.plainLanguage: The new document keeps the same lookup and adds a section of practical advice gathered from deployments, along with a default order value, a standard delimiter character and a new private-use marker for service types.

viz.caption: THE FOUR STEPS FROM NUMBER TO DOMAIN NAME (RFC 6116 SECTION 3.2)

data.title: First Well Known Rule
data.code:
1. Remove all characters with the exception of the digits.
   "+44-20-7946-0148"  ->  "442079460148"

2. Reverse the order of the digits.
   "442079460148"  ->  "841064970244"

3. Put dots ('.') between each digit.
   "841064970244"  ->  "8.4.1.0.6.4.9.7.0.2.4.4"

4. Append the string ".e164.arpa." to the end.
   "8.4.1.0.6.4.9.7.0.2.4.4.e164.arpa."

viz.caption: THE MARKERS AND FLAGS THE ENUM DATABASE USES

items.label: ENUM marker
items.desc: A non-optional prefix on the service field, denoting ENUM-only rewrite rules to mitigate record collisions.

items.label: Terminal flag
items.desc: The only flag defined so far. It means the rule is the last one and its output is a URI.

items.label: Experimental facet
items.desc: Reserved for experimental or trial use; such Enumservices cannot be registered by the normal process.

items.label: Private facet
items.desc: For private networks only. Never registered, and not to be provisioned where the public Internet can reach it.
